m3-t1.introduction: Build a content system around customer questions, not an empty posting calendar. Trace every piece back to a pillar, a stage and an owner.

sections.title: Strategy connects the topic, format and rhythm
sections.explanation: Three choices have to work together: what you explain, how the audience will use it and how often the team can deliver.

items.label: Topics
items.detail: Choose recurring questions tied to the offer.

items.label: Formats
items.detail: Use a guide, short video or comparison for a reason.

items.label: Cadence
items.detail: Choose a pace the team can sustain.

items.label: Outcome
items.detail: Define the useful action the content should support.

sections.takeaway: A calendar is the execution of a strategy; it is not the strategy itself.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Pillars make a connected library
sections.explanation: A pillar gives a broad subject a home. Cluster pieces answer narrower questions and link back into the same useful resource.

items.label: Choosing shoes
items.detail: Answer fit and use-case questions.

items.label: Starting a routine
items.detail: Explain a realistic first-week plan.

items.label: Avoiding mistakes
items.detail: Address common barriers without unsupported health claims.

items.label: Comparing options
items.detail: Help the customer evaluate suitable choices.

sections.takeaway: Choose clusters from research, not just from words an AI suggests.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Pillars and clusters: the structure of authority

sections.title: Match the format to the task
sections.explanation: A familiar format is not automatically the right format. Consider the information load and the reader’s next action.

items.label: Guide / article
items.detail: Useful when the customer needs a detailed searchable answer.

items.label: Short video
items.detail: Useful for one demonstration, hook or visual proof.

items.label: Carousel / checklist
items.detail: Useful for a sequence people can save and revisit.

items.label: Email
items.detail: Useful for a timely next step within an opted-in relationship.

sections.takeaway: The same topic can take different formats when each version does a distinct job.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Plan the mix, then leave capacity
sections.explanation: For a hypothetical 20-piece plan, a 60/30/10 mix gives 12 discovery, 6 consideration and 2 action pieces. It is a starting hypothesis, not a universal rule.

items.label: Discovery
items.detail: Answer broad questions and make the business familiar.

items.label: Consideration
items.detail: Offer comparisons, proof and deeper explanations.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Make a specific, appropriate next step clear.

sections.takeaway: In this example the team can produce 40 pieces but commits to 20. Keep owners, dates, distribution and a cut order visible.
sections.caption: Synthetic worked example, not live campaign data or an industry benchmark.

checkpoint.question: What should be cut first when a calendar becomes unmanageable?
checkpoint.answer: Use the pre-agreed cut order: remove low-value work that is least connected to audience needs and the goal. Protect quality, verification and distribution rather than simply publishing more.

m3-t2.introduction: AI speeds up parts of production, but the human owns the claim. Follow an editorial workflow with visible verification and a clear disclosure.

sections.title: Fluent text is not verified evidence
sections.explanation: A language model can generate a plausible sentence without knowing that its factual claim is correct.

items.label: Generate
items.detail: The model predicts a plausible continuation from its inputs.

items.label: Inspect
items.detail: A human identifies factual, numeric and sensitive claims.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Check authoritative sources or remove unsupported claims.

items.label: Own the result
items.detail: The publisher remains responsible for what goes live.

sections.takeaway: A more confident prompt is not a substitute for independent evidence.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. Why AI drafts hallucinate — and why prompting cannot fix it

sections.title: Five gates from brief to published piece
sections.explanation: A safe workflow separates drafting from verification. Save the trail, including what was corrected or removed.

items.label: Brief
items.detail: Specify audience, goal, facts, constraints and source material.

items.label: Draft
items.detail: Use AI for structure, variants or a first pass.

items.label: Verify
items.detail: Mark claims supported, false or unresolved.

items.label: Edit
items.detail: Improve accuracy, voice, usefulness and the next action.

items.label: Disclose
items.detail: State material AI use and human verification.

sections.takeaway: Unresolved claims do not become publishable because the prose looks finished.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: A voice sheet turns taste into guidance
sections.explanation: A small style sheet gives both people and tools a repeatable brand voice.

items.label: Voice anchors
items.detail: Name tone, audience language and approved examples.

items.label: Guardrails
items.detail: List banned claims, exaggerated promises and words to avoid.

items.label: Editing test
items.detail: Compare the draft with actual business language and evidence.

sections.takeaway: Ask for variants inside the voice constraints rather than asking AI to “make it viral”.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Brand voice: the style sheet trick

sections.title: Automate the low-risk friction
sections.explanation: Use AI where variation or organisation helps, and keep judgement where consequences are real.

items.label: Shape the message
items.detail: A human chooses the strongest accurate hook from draft variants.

items.label: Verify personally
items.detail: Claims about law, health, prices or results need evidence and approval.

items.label: Speed up formatting
items.detail: Reformat approved facts into a checklist or outline.

items.label: Do not auto-publish
items.detail: A fast workflow does not justify releasing unchecked sensitive claims.

sections.takeaway: Never upload confidential customer data merely to make the prompt more convenient.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: An AI draft invents a customer testimonial. Can you keep it if it sounds realistic?
checkpoint.answer: No. Remove it. A testimonial must come from a real, authorised source, and any customer-identifying material needs appropriate permission.

sections.section: 4. Where AI genuinely accelerates marketing content

m3-t3.introduction: See copy as a sequence of small decisions: earn attention, make the benefit concrete, support it and name one clear next step.

sections.title: A hook earns the next line
sections.explanation: A good hook is specific to a real audience problem. It makes an honest promise the rest of the copy can fulfil.

items.label: Generic hook
items.detail: “Best quality coaching for everyone” gives little useful information.

items.label: Specific hook
items.detail: “Working weekdays? Compare our weekend CA Foundation batches.”

sections.takeaway: Specificity attracts the right reader; exaggeration attracts the wrong expectation.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. The hook: earn the next second

sections.title: Climb the “so what?” ladder
sections.explanation: Move from a feature to its practical consequence, then to a benefit that matters in the customer’s situation.

items.label: Feature
items.detail: The class recording is available after the session.

items.label: Practical effect
items.detail: A learner can review a topic after work.

items.label: Customer benefit
items.detail: The course fits a busy schedule more comfortably.

items.label: Proof / limits
items.detail: State actual access duration and any restrictions.

sections.takeaway: A benefit is stronger when it is believable and supported, not merely emotional.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 2. Features tell, benefits sell — the "so what?" ladder

sections.title: Design for the scan
sections.explanation: Readers should understand the offer without reading every word. Put meaning into the hierarchy.

items.label: Headline
items.detail: State the useful promise.

items.label: Subhead / bullets
items.detail: Answer the main questions with evidence.

items.label: Proof
items.detail: Show a relevant example, source or genuine testimonial.

items.label: Action
items.detail: Give one appropriate next step.

sections.takeaway: The order should reduce uncertainty instead of hiding important information until the end.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Structure: make skimming the intended experience

sections.title: One page, one primary next step
sections.explanation: A CTA tells the reader what will happen after the click. Its wording should match the level of commitment.

items.label: Unclear action
items.detail: “Submit” does not explain what the person receives.

items.label: Clear action
items.detail: “View weekend batch timings” names the result.

items.label: Honest expectation
items.detail: Explain whether the action opens a page or requests a callback.

sections.takeaway: A misleading button may create clicks while reducing trust and lead quality.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 4. The call to action: name the next step

sections.title: Clarity beats inflated language
sections.explanation: Replace vague praise with useful facts that a customer can check.

items.label: Inflated
items.detail: “Revolutionary, world-class solutions” hides the actual offer.

items.label: Clear
items.detail: “A 30-minute consultation to compare two course options” names scope and time.

sections.takeaway: Plain language is not a lack of personality. It makes the promise easier to understand and evaluate.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Why can “View fees and batch timings” outperform “Click here” as a useful CTA?
checkpoint.answer: It names the result and reduces uncertainty. Whether it improves conversion needs testing with the right audience; clear wording is a starting principle, not a guaranteed uplift.

m3-t4.introduction: Give a useful original piece a second life without copying it blindly. Build distribution, feedback and a stop rule into the workflow.

sections.title: One source, several native versions
sections.explanation: Repurposing keeps the core idea but changes the shape to fit each channel and audience.

items.label: Short video
items.detail: Demonstrate one practical point with a clear hook.

items.label: Carousel
items.detail: Turn the sequence into a saveable checklist.

items.label: Email
items.detail: Explain why this matters now and link to the full guide.

items.label: Community answer
items.detail: Use the relevant insight to answer a real question.

sections.takeaway: Each asset must make sense on its own and preserve the source’s factual limits.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 1. Create once, distribute everywhere — the waterfall

sections.title: Publishing starts the distribution job
sections.explanation: A live URL is not a distribution plan. Put the asset where the intended audience can appropriately discover it.

items.label: Publish
items.detail: Check the page, link and CTA work.

items.label: Distribute
items.detail: Use relevant owned channels and appropriate communities.

items.label: Respond
items.detail: Answer genuine questions and record objections.

items.label: Record
items.detail: Log the date, source tags and useful outcomes.

sections.takeaway: Do not spam groups or message people who have not agreed to that use of their contact details.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Make the feedback loop visible
sections.explanation: A good result suggests a question for the next piece, not an excuse to duplicate content forever.

items.label: Observe
items.detail: Check saves, qualified clicks and enquiries in context.

items.label: Explain
items.detail: Ask what the topic, hook or format helped people do.

items.label: Adapt
items.detail: Create a new version that tests the explanation.

items.label: Compare
items.detail: Use the same definitions and a comparable window.

sections.takeaway: More posts are not the same as more learning. Keep the reason for each iteration visible.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.
sections.section: 3. Iteration beats volume: make more of what worked

sections.title: Choose continue, revise or stop in advance
sections.explanation: A kill rule protects limited time. It needs a fair observation window and a metric tied to the asset’s purpose.

items.label: Continue
items.detail: Evidence supports the job the asset was meant to do.

items.label: Revise
items.detail: The audience is relevant but a hook, answer or CTA is weak.

items.label: Stop / replace
items.detail: After a fair test, the asset repeatedly misses the agreed useful outcome.

sections.takeaway: Do not kill educational content because it lacks immediate sales if its agreed role is consideration.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: Is copying the same caption to five platforms meaningful repurposing?
checkpoint.answer: Not usually. Adapt the hook, format, context and CTA for each channel while keeping the core evidence accurate. Also plan how the asset will actually reach people.

m3-pb2.introduction: See the content engine as a complete production and learning loop. Keep the verification trail beside the published work, not hidden in a draft folder.

sections.title: The engine needs publication and feedback
sections.explanation: Planning, production and distribution become a system when a real audience can respond.

items.label: Research / plan
items.detail: Link topics to the audience, pillars and business goal.

items.label: Draft / verify
items.detail: Preserve the brief, draft, claim checks and edit.

items.label: Publish / distribute
items.detail: Release the approved piece and channel-native versions.

items.label: Read / decide
items.detail: Use available evidence to choose the next iteration.

sections.takeaway: A hypothetical unpublished piece does not fulfil the published-piece requirement.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Keep the submission as an inspectable trail
sections.explanation: The assessor should be able to trace a published claim back to its source and the editorial decision.

items.label: Strategy
items.detail: One-line strategy, pillar map and 30-day calendar.

items.label: Production
items.detail: Brief, AI draft, claim-by-claim checks and final version.

items.label: Copy + publication
items.detail: Hooks, benefit ladder, CTA and a real publication record.

items.label: Distribution
items.detail: At least three repurposed assets and a dated checklist.

items.label: Learning
items.detail: Two-week readout, reflection and specific AI-use statement.

sections.takeaway: Save links and screenshots in a clear order so an assessor does not have to reconstruct the workflow.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Use a pre-flight gate for the content engine
sections.explanation: Coverage requirements test the system, not only the polish of the final post.

items.label: Calendar gate
items.detail: Mix stages, name formats and show spare capacity.

items.label: Safety gate
items.detail: Show a claim corrected or removed and disclose AI use.

items.label: Action gate
items.detail: The published piece has one clear CTA.

items.label: Distribution gate
items.detail: The waterfall includes a channel new to your practice.

sections.takeaway: Never add a false claim to a live post just to demonstrate verification. Check and remove the risky draft claim before publication.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Sequence the work so feedback has time to arrive
sections.explanation: Choose and publish the first piece early enough to collect the readout requested in the brief.

items.label: Plan
items.detail: Choose pillars, calendar and the first useful piece.

items.label: Publish safely
items.detail: Complete the verification and disclosure workflow.

items.label: Peer review
items.detail: Ask a partner to challenge the claim trail.

items.label: Distribute / read
items.detail: Finish the waterfall and report the actual observation window.

sections.takeaway: If the full readout window is not available, label the dates and consult the facilitator rather than inventing results.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

sections.title: Show the system as well as the artefact
sections.explanation: The rubric rewards the reasoning and evidence behind the final content.

items.label: Coherence
items.detail: Research, copy and formats support a clear strategy.

items.label: Reality and safety
items.detail: The piece is published with a visible verification trail.

items.label: Sustainability
items.detail: Distribution, capacity, stop rules and learning are documented.

sections.takeaway: The original rubric controls assessment. These groups do not change its criteria or weights.
sections.caption: Concept illustration, not a platform screenshot. Follow the labels and the relationships shown.

checkpoint.question: What proves responsible AI-assisted production beyond a polished final article?
checkpoint.answer: The brief, draft, claim-by-claim evidence checks, corrections, final human edit and a specific AI-use statement. Include the real publication and distribution record too.
